procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 2nd June, 2011 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in Criminal Miscellaneous No.M-2829 of 2011.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh, relying on a previous judgment of the same court and the settlement of a dispute, quashed the criminal proceedings against the respondents (FIR No.SIA-2001-E-0006 dated 28.12.2001 under Sections 420 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, registered at Police Station, SIU(X)/SPE/CBI, New Delhi) and the criminal proceedings pending in the Court of learned Special Judicial Magistrate, CBI, Punjab, Patiala.

directions: Keep the said point of law open.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 482 of Cr.P.C., can quash an FIR and consequential proceedings for non-compoundable offences based on a settlement between the complainant and the accused.

facts: An FIR was registered against the respondents for non-compoundable offences of cheating and forgery (Sections 420 and 471 IPC).
During the proceedings, the respondents (accused) and the complainant Bank reached a compromise under a One Time Settlement scheme.
The Trial Court dismissed an application to compound the offences, noting that they were non-compoundable under the law.
The respondents then approached the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR and subsequent proceedings based on the settlement.
The High Court, relying on a previous Full Bench judgment, allowed the petition and quashed the criminal proceedings.
law: Section 320 of the Cr.P.C. specifies which offences are compoundable (can be settled by parties) and which are not.
Section 320(9) of the Cr.P.C. explicitly states that no offence shall be compounded except as provided by that section, creating a legal prohibition.
Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. grants High Courts inherent power to prevent the abuse of the process of court or to secure the ends of justice.

The Supreme Court cited the doctrine of judicial restraint, which suggests that courts should not do something indirectly (quashing based on settlement) that they are expressly prohibited from doing directly (compounding a non-compoundable offence).

The Court also acknowledged a counter-principle from other judgments: that continuing criminal proceedings after a compromise can sometimes amount to an abuse of the court's process and an exercise in futility, especially if a conviction is unlikely.
application: The Supreme Court established that while the High Court has the power under Section 482, it should not be used to indirectly bypass the prohibition in Section 320(9) Cr.P.C.
The Court held that the power to quash proceedings for non-compoundable offences must be exercised with great caution and depends on the specific facts and circumstances of each case.
It is not a legitimate exercise of judicial power to quash proceedings for serious offences or those with a wider societal impact simply because the parties have settled.
In this specific case, the Supreme Court found that the High Court had erred by ignoring crucial factors, such as the serious impact of the alleged fraud and the conduct of the accused.

The Court concluded that considering the nature of the offences (cheating and forgery against a bank), this was not an appropriate case for the High Court to exercise its inherent power to quash the proceedings, despite the settlement.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a High Court can, in certain exceptional circumstances, exercise its power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash proceedings for non-compoundable offences based on a settlement. However, this power must be used with judicial restraint and is not a blanket rule. The court must consider the nature and gravity of the offence and its societal impact. In this particular case, given the seriousness of the fraud allegations, the Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in quashing the proceedings and therefore set aside its judgment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 482 of Cr.P.C., can quash an FIR and consequential proceedings for non-compoundable offences based on a settlement between the complainant and the accused.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (CBI) argued that the High Court cannot quash an FIR for non-compoundable offences based on a settlement.

The appellant cited three Supreme Court decisions to support this argument: Mwwj S/wrnw Vs. Stale & Ors., (2008) 16 SCC I; Central Bureau of Investi1.:atio11 Vs. A. Ravislumkar Prasad & Ors., (2009) 6 SCC 351; and Central Bureau of J11vestif(lltio11 Vs. Mll11i11der Si11f(h, (2016) 1 SCC 389.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the High Court judiciously and rightly considered the facts and circumstances of the case and was correct in quashing the FIR.
The respondent contended that the offences in the present case are not heinous.

The respondent relied on the Supreme Court's judgment in Gian Singh Vs. Stllte of Pu11jllb & Anr., (2012) 10 SCC 303, and a Full Bench judgment of the High Court in Ku/winder Singh & Ors. Vs. Stllte of Punjllb &Anr. to support the High Court's power to quash the proceedings.

cases.case_name: State of Tamil Nadu v. R. Vasanthi Stanley & Anr.
cases.principle: Encroaching into the right of the other organ of the government would tantamount to a clear violation of the rule of law, which is one of the basic structures of the Constitution of India.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Encroaching into the right of the other organ of the government would tantamount to a clear violation of the rule of law which is one of the basic structures of the Constitution of India.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court explicitly declined to rule on the general point of law regarding the High Court's power to quash non-compoundable offences based on a settlement. Instead, it dismissed the appeal based on the specific, unstated facts of the case, thereby leaving the legal question open for future determination.
legal_tests_applied: The exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. would entirely depend on the facts and circumstances of each case, with the object being to prevent abuse of the process of the court or to secure the ends of justice.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant lost because the court, despite acknowledging the principle of judicial restraint, ultimately decided the case on its specific facts, finding that dismissing the appeal was the proper course of action in this particular instance without setting a general precedent.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld on the specific facts of the case, as the court was 'not unmindful of the view... that depending on the attendant facts, continuance of the criminal proceedings, after a compromise has been arrived at between the complainant and the accused, would amount to abuse of process of Court and an exercise in futility since the trial would be prolonged and ultimately, it may end in a decision which may be of no consequence to any of the parties.'
policy_considerations: The court emphasized the doctrine of judicial restraint and separation of powers, stating that 'encroaching into the right of the other organ of the government would tantamount clear violation of the rule of law which is one of the basic structure of the Constitution oflndia.'

The court considered the practical futility of continuing criminal proceedings after a compromise, noting that 'the trial would be prolonged and ultimately, it may end in a decision which may be of no consequence to any of the parties.'

The court acknowledged a competing policy concern that simply quashing a matter because it has been settled 'can never be an acc.eptable principle or para111ete1~ for that would amount to destroying the stem cells of law and order in many a realm and further strengthen the marrows of the unscrupulous litigations.'
